why: This is the BST invariant itself: every key in a left subtree is below its ancestor and every key in a right subtree is above it. Equivalently, an in-order walk of a valid BST is strictly increasing, so you check that one sequence instead of comparing each node with its parent only.
hints: Checking only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val is not enough: a deep node must also respect every ancestor above it.
Either pass down an allowed open interval (low, high) and tighten it at each step, or walk the tree in order and require each value to be strictly greater than the previous one.
Iterative in-order traversal with an explicit stack and a 'previous value' variable: O(n) time, O(h) extra space, and no recursion-depth trouble on a 10,000-node chain.
pitfalls: Equal values are invalid: the rule is strictly smaller / strictly larger.
Values can be the 32-bit extremes, so do not use -2^31 or 2^31-1 as sentinels; use None or infinity.
A skewed tree of 10,000 nodes overflows Python's default recursion limit.
statement:
You are given the root of a binary tree. Return true if it is a valid binary search tree, otherwise false.

A tree is a valid BST when, for every node:

  • every value in its left subtree is strictly smaller than the node's value;
  • every value in its right subtree is strictly larger than the node's value.

The rule applies to all descendants, not only direct children.

Example. root = [2,1,3]: the root 2 has left child 1 < 2 and right child 3 > 2, and both children are leaves. The in-order sequence is 1, 2, 3, strictly increasing, so the answer is true.

By contrast, [5,1,6,null,null,4,7] is not valid: 4 is the left child of 6 (fine locally) but sits in the right subtree of 5 while being smaller than 5.
